Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-04
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Ortiz (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood PM); Samir Patel (Novus - Head of ML Infra), Lena Zhou (Novus - SRE), Tom Reed (Novus - AI Platform), Aisha Khan (Novus - Research)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be noisy):
Redwood and Novus walked through hybrid sharding options for MoE models, cost modeling for routing and token affinity, RoPE scaling impacts on long-context workloads, and a plan for quant-pruning experiments. Action items: Redwood to run bench sims and share CSVs; Novus to provide prompt set and deployment constraints; follow-up for VPC canary.

Topics: hybrid sharding, MoE routing costs, shard affinity, RoPE scaling/decay, KV-cache prewarm/pinning, microbatch vs continuous batching, quant pruning (post train and QAT), VPC/on-prem deployment constraints.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: All right good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. we're gonna dig into the hybrid sharding and MoE token economics, the goal is to come out with a clear next step for a canary test on Novus's 16 GPU pod.
[00:12] Samir Patel: Yep thanks Maya, high level we want to understand if MoE routing is going to blow the per-token cost for our summarization pipeline, we have long context docs usually 6k to 10k tokens, and we care about 95th percentile latency.
[00:25] Carlos Ortiz: Cool. quick qualifier — what's current infra? are you running everything on prem with Inference-as-a-Service, or cloud VMs?
[00:32] Lena Zhou: We're mostly on-prem right now, a private rack with 16x A100 80G equivalent, connected via Infiniband. we do have a VPC test env. routing is via our homegrown router.
[00:44] Tom Reed: We do tenant isolation via namespace and some custom RBAC, but network egress rules are strict.
[00:50] Maya Chen: Good. that's in line with what we've seen. so we'll talk dedicated vs private tradeoffs briefly — but mainly we'll focus on runtime knobs: RoPE scaling, KV-cache prewarm and shard affinity tables, microbatch sizing and continuous batching, and quant-pruning strategies.
[01:06] Aisha Khan: Quick question — when you say "RoPE scaling" do you mean adjusting positional decay for long contexts, or actually changing the RoPE frequency/scale factor?
[01:14] Carlos Ortiz: both, sort of. there are two levers: the RoPE frequency/scale (people sometimes call it rope-scaling) which preserves relative position across long spans, and positional decay tuning which mitigates catastrophic drift in attention as sequences grow. they interact with KV cache effectiveness.
[01:28] Samir Patel: We're also worried about token affinity — a lot of requests have repeated prefixes and the KV cache hit rate could be high, but with MoE routing the gating may send tokens to different experts over time, invalidating prefix cache.
[01:40] Priya Nair: that's a great callout. Carlos, for hybrid sharding, we suggested model-parallel for experts and data-parallel for the dense parts — can you sketch cost model quick?
[01:50] Carlos Ortiz: Sure. simple model: cost per token = base_dense_cost + expert_cost * expert_invocation_rate. expert_invocation_rate is function of gating sparsity and top_k. overheads: cross-node allreduce for expert logits, extra KV cache sharding and prewarm, and increased network egress if experts hosted on separate shards. For your setup, dense cost is roughly 0.8x of a comparable dense-only run because tensor core kernels are similar; but experts add 0.15-0.6x depending on branching.
[02:18] Tom Reed: okay numbers please, ballpark.
[02:20] Carlos Ortiz: ballpark for 80G A100 pods — dense-only 13ms per token at our optimized runtime for Mistral-like dense model. with MoE 1%, meaning 1 expert activation per token on average, add ~4-8ms due to routing and remote KV ops. if activation is 3-4% becomes 15-20ms extra. so tail latency matters.
[02:38] Samir Patel: those are significant. how much can batching help? our traffic is bursty but we can accept a few ms of added latency if cost drops.
[02:47] Carlos Ortiz: Microbatching + continuous batching helps amortize kernel launches for experts, but MoE gating is often per-token and can break batching granularity. our runtime supports adaptive batching: it will batch tokens with same routing signature (shard affinity) and route them together. that requires tracking a small routing fingerprint — it can reduce per-expert overhead by 30-50% if your token distribution has locality.
[03:09] Lena Zhou: Routing fingerprint — is that stable across different prefixes? because we often have prompt templates that shuffle tokens.
[03:16] Carlos Ortiz: it's heuristic — we use a cheap LRU on last N tokens; if gating changes because of small prompt edits, fingerprint will drift. that's where KV-cache pinning comes in: if you pin a prefix to a particular expert shard for k steps, you'll get higher cache hits but risk suboptimal gating. it's a tradeoff.
[03:31] Maya Chen: Also quant-pruning — Novus mentioned wanting int4 for cost. we talked previously about QA training vs post-training quantization. which is feasible for your models?
[03:39] Samir Patel: we prefer post-train because we don't have compute for QAT on our entire fleet — but open to partial QAT for experts only.
[03:46] Carlos Ortiz: we've prototyped hybrid quant-pruning: prune low-importance weights in the experts then run symmetric int8->int4 post-train quant with a small calibration set. that gets ~1.2-1.5x speed-up on GPU kernels with minimal quality drop for classification-ish tasks; generative tasks can be sensitive — but pruning experts first reduces gating noise and helps quant.
[04:05] Aisha Khan: how do you measure "minimal"? do you run eval prompts?
[04:08] Priya Nair: yes, Redwood Optimize integrates evals per-prompt-set. for Novus we'll suggest a small eval set representing your topo: summarization, extraction, and dialogue. Carlos, do we have an example CSV?
[04:19] Carlos Ortiz: yes I'll attach a sample run later but high level: measure per-token perplexity shift, downstream ROUGE/quality metrics, and latency/cost. recommend canary thresholds: perplexity < 2% delta and ROUGE < 1.5% drop.
[04:35] Samir Patel: ROUGE is noisy but ok.
[04:38] Tom Reed: network egress — if experts live on remote shards we need to ensure intra-rack bandwidth doesn't saturate. how does Redwood handle fallbacks if a shard is slow?
[04:47] Maya Chen: runtime has graceful-deg fallback: we can reroute to a dense fallback or to a smaller local replica. you can set policy: latency-first or cost-first. for latency-first, if expert RPC exceeds threshold, route to local dense variant. that adds some quality variance but keeps SLAs.
[05:02] Lena Zhou: can we pin some experts locally so critical prefixes never cross rack boundary?
[05:06] Carlos Ortiz: yes — shard affinity table. we can pre-assign hot experts to local GPUs based on profiling. discuss: do you want static pinning or adaptive pinning?
[05:15] Samir Patel: we prefer adaptive, because traffic changes per-run. but adaptive is complex. what's the overhead?
[05:22] Carlos Ortiz: adaptive requires telemetry and a small control plane; we've built a lightweight agent that monitors top-k tokens and migrates shard hints during low load windows. migration cost is mostly metadata updates; real state transfer only if you physically move an expert replica. we usually avoid moving large weights; instead we spin up a secondary replica in the target rack when needed.
[05:40] Aisha Khan: spinning up replicas costs commit capacity. do we have a hybrid where you overprovision small fraction for hot experts?
[05:46] Carlos Ortiz: yes we recommend a tiny hot-replica pool for the top ~5% heaviest experts. that covers burst tails.
[05:52] Maya Chen: moving on to KV-cache prewarm: your summarization workload has long prefixes — prewarming large prefix caches helps but can increase memory pressure. what's your average context window?
[06:02] Samir Patel: 6k tokens typical, but sometimes up to 12k.
[06:06] Carlos Ortiz: for 12k contexts, full KV cache for all layers can be huge; strategies: selective layer caching (top 6 layers), prefix sampling, or compressed KV (float16->int8 compress). Redwood runtime supports compressed-kv on the fly with decompression kernels. that cuts memory by ~2x at cost of ~1ms decompression per prewarm chunk.
[06:27] Lena Zhou: interesting. decompression overhead seems acceptable. does compression affect RoPE behavior?
[06:31] Carlos Ortiz: not directly; but if you compress and tone down RoPE scaling you may change attention distribution. so you have to calibrate together.
[06:38] Priya Nair: let's discuss an experiment plan — what Redwood will run for Novus and what Novus will supply.
[06:44] Maya Chen: propose three staged experiments: 1) offline cost sim: Redwood runs hybrid-shard cost model using your traffic distribution and sample prompts; 2) quant-prune bench: Redwood runs post-train quant with expert pruning on a small eval set; 3) VPC canary: deploy hybrid-shard with hotspot replicas and adaptive shard affinity to your VPC test cluster.
[07:02] Samir Patel: timeline?
[07:04] Maya Chen: 1) cost sim within 5 business days — Carlos will run; 2) quant-prune bench within 7-10 days — Carlos + Priya; 3) VPC canary week of 2026-11-15 pending your prompt corpus and access.
[07:16] Carlos Ortiz: for the offline sim I'll need: token distribution, average request concurrency, and a small calibration sample of 200 prompts. Samir can you share?
[07:24] Samir Patel: yes, we'll push that by 2026-11-09.
[07:27] Aisha Khan: one more thing — security: we require HSM integration for key wrap in our production. is that supported for private deployments?
[07:34] Maya Chen: yes Redwood Private supports KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs. I'll send the SOC2 + ISO docs.
[07:40] Tom Reed: ping on licensing costs — if we increase hot replica pool that's capacity commit right?
[07:45] Maya Chen: correct, Dedicated/Private has reserved capacity options. for a small hot-pool it's usually an incremental capacity add-on. I'll include pricing scenarios in the follow-up.
[07:53] Samir Patel: about fallback quality — have you seen systematic failure modes when routing to dense fallback?
[07:58] Carlos Ortiz: Yes two main failure modes: gating mismatch causing hallucination shifts, and distributional shift because dense rep was trained differently. mitigation: use a lightweight reranker or confidence threshold; additionally Redwood Optimize can trigger a fallback only when reranker score is above threshold.
[08:15] Lena Zhou: for the quant-prune bench will you run on our actual 80G kernels or on mock nodes?
[08:20] Carlos Ortiz: we can run on Redwood's lab 80G pods and also emulate network constraints similar to your rack. if you want exact parity we'll coordinate to run the canary in your VPC.
[08:29] Priya Nair: quick note — calibration set for quant should include long-context docs, because int4 tends to degrade on very long dependency chains.
[08:37] Aisha Khan: any tips for prompt engineering to reduce expert churn? we could alter prompts to make gating more stable.
[08:44] Carlos Ortiz: yes, canonicalization helps a lot: normalize casing, templates, prefix anchors. also keep deterministic separators so gating sees similar token patterns. that can increase KV-hit by 10-20%.
[08:56] Samir Patel: are there any automatic tools to canonicalize at runtime?
[08:59] Maya Chen: Redwood exposes pre-processor hooks you can plug into at the route level — simple regex transforms, tokenization normalization, and a small ML-based normalizer.
[09:09] Tom Reed: last technical question: RoPE scaling breaks positional locality assumptions for some models; does Redwood runtime support per-layer RoPE overrides?
[09:18] Carlos Ortiz: yes — you can set RoPE scale per layer or per head in advanced configs. we saw good results by scaling only mid layers for extraction tasks. but it's model-specific — we'll include suggested configs for Llama/Mistral/Qwen families.
[09:33] Maya Chen: ok let's recap next steps and owners.
[09:36] Maya Chen: Carlos to run cost sim and quant-prune bench (due 2026-11-11). Samir to provide prompt corpus and traffic metrics (due 2026-11-09). Maya to send security docs and pricing (due 2026-11-06). schedule canary for week of 2026-11-15 once we have corpora.
[09:51] Samir Patel: thanks. couple of small notes — please include expected p95 latency numbers for dense fallback scenarios.
[09:57] Carlos Ortiz: will do, I'll include CSVs with p50/p95/p99 and per-expert hit rates.
[10:04] Aisha Khan: thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[10:07] End meeting.
